sources.headline: Venezuela's ex-leader Nicolás Maduro charged with conspiracy to commit torture
sources.text: Prosecutors in the United States have accused Venezuela's former leader Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, of conspiracy to commit torture. The fresh charges against the couple were made public on Thursday and are in addition to the drug-trafficking and weapons charges already brought against them, which they have denied. Maduro, 63, and Flores, 69, have been in custody since January in a detention centre in Brooklyn, where they were taken after US forces seized them in a pre-dawn raid on their compound in the Venezuelan capital, Caracas. Barry J Pollack, Maduro's attorney, said his client denies the new charges and looks forward to his day in court.Federal prosecutors also announced on Thursday that Flores was added to the earlier narco-terrorism charge.The trial for both Maduro and Flores is set to begin in June 2027. Both are being held in a detention centre in Brooklyn and are expected to remain there after Flores's request to be moved to house arrest was denied by a judge on Thursday.The new accusations relate to the alleged torture of US citizens who were being held in Venezuela while Maduro was in power.The superseding indictment unsealed on Thursday accuses the former presidential couple of "entrenching themselves in power" by presiding "over a system of repression that relied on violence against political opposition, arbitrary detention, and the torture of detainees, including United States citizens". According to the indictment, the torture included "electric shock, asphyxiation, rape, forced nudity, prolonged isolation, starvation, punishment cells, and psychological torture".The prosecutors allege that the psychological torture included threats to kill victims' families, including children. "All of this was done to ensure that Maduro and Flores retained their power," prosecutors said outside the courthouse on Thursday. "This conduct, we allege, has caused significant harm to Americans, to US citizens", prosecutors said, calling it "the epitome of corruption".The prosecution accuses Flores of having played a key role in the development of the repressive system, ordering that individuals be tortured and even receiving updates on the torture of specific prisoners.The court document alleges that she did so in order to protect members of her family who were involved in illegal activities. The allegations contained in the superseding indictment echo many of the accusations long made by prisoners who have been released from detention in Venezuela.Javier Tarazona, the head of a human rights group in Venezuela, told BBC Mundo's Norberto Paredes earlier this year how he and his brother were held in a tiny punishment cell for 46 days after being arbitrarily arrested. Another former inmate, Ángel Godoy, told BBC Mundo that he was kept isolated for months and not allowed to contact his wife, who was in turn kept in the dark about his whereabouts. The allegations listed in the superseding indictment made public on Thursday relate to cases during Maduro's time in power.After his ouster, his vice-president, Delcy Rodríguez, was sworn in as interim leader with the backing of the Trump administration.While hundreds of political prisoners have been released under an amnesty law since she has taken over power, more than 300 still remain behind bars, according to prisoners' rights group Foro Penal.The United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk has warned that his office has received reports alleging that detainees continue to be tortured even after the seizure of Maduro. Türk said in March that "structural and systemic human rights concerns" had persisted in Venezuela despite Maduro's ousting.Venezuela's foreign minister at the time accused Türk of parroting the agenda of "extremists" by citing the allegations.

sources.headline: Nicolás Maduro and his wife indicted for alleged torture of US citizens
sources.text: The deposed Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, have been indicted for alleged conspiracy to commit torture, according to Manhattan federal court papers unsealed on Thursday.The superseding indictment was unsealed shortly before Flores appeared at court in her ongoing push for pretrial release – which was denied by Judge Alvin Hellerstein. Maduro and Flores have been jailed in New York City since early January.They were captured by US special forces during a shocking predawn assault on Caracas and transported to New York to face “narcoterrorism”-related charges in a move that sparked widespread international outrage. Charging documents at the time alleged that Maduro spearheaded a “corrupt, illegitimate government that, for decades, has leveraged government power to protect and promote illegal activity, including drug trafficking”.Maduro and Flores have previously pleaded not guilty in the criminal case against them. CNN on Wednesday first reported that a new indictment was expected.The new charging document described how Maduro and his wife allegedly wielded untold horrors to suppress opposition and maintain their control.Maduro, Flores and other Venezuelan leaders “presided over a system of repression that relied on violence against political opposition, arbitrary detention, and the torture of detainees, including United States citizens”, the just-released charging document said.Maduro and Flores, the superseding indictment alleged, “sat atop that violent power structure”. They allegedly “developed and facilitated the systems which they and their co-conspirators used corruptly to amass immense wealth and power, rewarding allies with ill-gotten funds and terrorizing perceived opponents through persecution and violence”.Flores was integral to this effort, authorities claimed, saying she “helped develop this system of repression and ordered that individuals be tortured to protect her family members’ illegal activities”.The victims of their torture included US citizens “who were believed to pose a threat” to Maduro’s power.“One particular United States citizen was detained in Venezuela and subjected to, among other things, deprivation of food and water, simulated drowning, repeated beatings, electric shock to his testicles, and forced injections.”Maduro and Flores also put pressure on Venezuela’s judiciary to make legal decisions that supported their efforts to thwart opposition, charging papers alleged. When one official resisted, Venezuelan intelligence agents arrested and tortured their family members, charging papers stated.“For example, one family member … was forced to drink latrine water; assaulted with tear gas in Victim-1’s cell; threatened that Victim-1 would be killed at gunpoint; and placed in a cold room known as the ‘Freezer’ in which a bright light was left on at all times of day and night and music was blared on repeat,” the superseding indictment said.This official “ultimately … relented and blocked the opposition figures from running for political office”.During another alleged torture incident, authorities allegedly abused the friend of a suspected opponent by “asphyxiating him with a bag, applying electric shocks to his testicles and knees, and kicking and beating him with a blunt object”, court papers said.One torture victim, who was repeatedly interrogated, endured numerous threats “including that his daughter would be kidnapped and raped if he did not confess and name his supposed confederates”, court papers state. “On one occasion, interrogators produced women’s underwear, claiming it belonged to his daughter.”Shortly after this indictment surfaced, Flores’s attorneys argued for her release in an already scheduled proceeding, pitching house arrest guarded by 24-hour private security. In doing so, they invoked chronic health issues, including cardiac infirmities.Hellerstein pushed back on this claim, noting that Flores was refusing to have catheterization while detained in general population.skip past newsletter promotionafter newsletter promotion“I’ve undergone it, so I know what it is,” Hellerstein said, noting that it was generally an outpatient procedure. “There’s no pain. There’s no general anesthesia.”Flores’s attorney then pointed to her high blood pressure. “It’s controllable by pills,” Hellerstein said.Her team also said in court that Flores dropped more than 25lbs and lost two teeth since her detention.“For whatever it’s worth, her appearance today is no worse than, and perhaps a little better, than when I first met with her [at] her arraignment,” Hellerstein said. Flores’s lawyer said that during her arraignment she was “still bandaged up” from her rough arrest. Flores wore dark jail scrubs during her court appearance. She listened to the proceedings with headphones through a Spanish-language interpreter.The US attorney’s office for the southern district of New York, which is prosecuting this case, opposed Flores’s now-failed bail request. Prosecutors have argued that Flores was a flight risk. Prosecutors also maintained that she had received appropriate medical care.Donald Trump has defended the controversial raid on Maduro, insisting it was a “surgical law enforcement operation”. At Maduro’s first US court appearance, he said: “I’m a kidnapped president – a prisoner of war!”After Maduro’s forced ouster, Trump worked swiftly to gain access to Venezuela’s expansive oil reserves. In August, Trump announced a new oil agreement with Venezuela – claiming that the US would have “majority” control over 65bn barrels of proven reserves.Venezuela boasts approximately 303bn barrels of proven oil reserves – the largest in the world. The White House has tried establishing a consistent flow of Venezuelan crude oil to US refineries while boosting US investment into the country’s flagging petroleum industry.Trump has faced mounting pressure over skyrocketing gas prices in advance of November’s midterm elections. Greater access to cheaper oil and broadened output could help lower costs.A Guardian investigation found, however, that Trump’s proclaimed “biggest oil deal in world history” is likely to fail due to legal and logistical problems.

sources.headline: US charges Venezuela’s Nicolas Maduro over torture allegations
US charges former Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro with torture
sources.text:
Published on
08/10/2026 - 18:20 GMT+2
US authorities charged former Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, on Thursday with conspiring to torture Venezuelan citizens to remain in power.
“He authorized the use of torture against specific individuals and oversaw a system designed to use torture, arbitrary detention and violence as a means of repression against the political opposition,” says the revised indictment.
The indictment alleges that thousands of Venezuelans were “harassed, threatened, arrested, prosecuted, assaulted, tortured, or killed” by people acting on behalf of Maduro’s government.
The alleged abuse included electric shocks, beatings and asphyxiation. Maduro is also accused of approving torture methods and personally threatening to kill a prisoner’s child “as a form of psychological torture.”
The indictment alleges that the torture victims included three US citizens, who were not named in the court documents.
The new indictment adds to the legal pressure on Maduro, who already faces charges of conspiring to smuggle cocaine into the US. He now also faces allegations of human rights abuses committed during his presidency.
Maduro and Flores, have been detained in New York since January, after US forces captured them during an overnight raid on their Caracas home.
Both have pleaded not guilty to drug trafficking charges and could face life imprisonment if convicted.
Maduro has also been under investigation by the International Criminal Court for alleged crimes against humanity linked to his crackdown on political opponents. He has consistently denied wrongdoing.

sources.headline: New U.S. indictment charges former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro with torture
sources.text:
Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores wave after his swearing-in ceremony for a third term at the National Assembly in Caracas, Venezuela, on Jan. 10, 2025.
Ariana Cubillos/AP
hide caption
Ariana Cubillos/AP
NEW YORK — U.S. authorities added new torture charges Thursday to their case against former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, ramping up pressure on the ousted authoritarian leader already fighting drug trafficking allegations. Maduro and wife Cilia Flores, already charged with participating in a conspiracy to send cocaine into the U.S., now also face allegations of human rights abuses during his time as president of the oil-rich South American nation.
The updated indictment "alleges conduct that is truly unthinkable," New York-based U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald said outside the courthouse where the case is being handled. He said thousands of Venezuelans, and some Americans, were tortured to ensure that Maduro and Flores held onto power. "This is the epitome of corruption," McDonald said. The allegations include electric shocks, beatings and asphyxiation at Maduro's behest. Maduro, the indictment claims, signed off on torture methods, sought and got updates on specific victims' treatment, watched a video of a forced confession and personally threatened the killing of one prisoner's child "as a form of psychological torture."
Flores, a former legislator and attorney general, helped develop the repressive system and ordered the torture of some specific people, the indictment contends. A message seeking comment was sent to Maduro's lawyer. Flores' attorney said he hadn't yet had time to review the new allegations. The couple pleaded not guilty in the U.S. drug case first brought years ago against them and numerous alleged co-conspirators. Their attorneys have asked for the case to be dismissed on the grounds that they have immunity as the leader and first lady of a foreign country.
They face potential sentences of life in prison if convicted. Maduro, who served as Venezuela's president from 2013 until his capture in January, has been under investigation for years by the International Criminal Court over allegations of crimes against humanity, tied to his crackdown on opponents. He has always denied any wrongdoing. Both Maduro and Flores have been behind bars in New York since early January, when forces seized them from their Caracas home in a middle-of-the-night raid. Flores' lawyers unsuccessfully asked a judge Thursday to release her on house arrest. Outside the courthouse, over a dozen demonstrators chanted slogans and held signs supporting her request. Alleged torture victims included U.S. citizens The revised indictment includes several mentions of the involvement of Venezuela's feared DGCIM military intelligence agency, which was headed for many years by one of Maduro's co-defendants, Gen. Hugo Carvajal. He broke with Maduro years ago, pleaded guilty last year to drug trafficking charges in New York and has offered to testify against his former boss.
While the indictment doesn't name the alleged torture victims, three are described as U.S. citizens. One was punched, subjected to electric shocks and forced to eat his own vomit during eight months of imprisonment, the indictment says. Another was beaten badly enough to necessitate a long hospital stay and had a gun stuck in his mouth. A third was handcuffed, hooded and beaten for two days every half an hour, suffering a permanent eye injury, the indictment said. Maduro has long ignored lawsuits brought in U.S. courts by Americans who alleged they were beaten while in custody in Venezuela. Among those who sued is Matthew Heath, a former U.S. Marine corporal from Tennessee. He was arrested at a roadblock in Venezuela in 2020 and held in custody for more than two years. In May, Heath and another former prisoner won a $300 million default judgment against Maduro and other top Venezuelan officials for overseeing a pattern of torture. The lawsuit, brought under a federal anti-terrorism law, included allegations of waterboarding, electrocution, threats of rape with a nightstick, administration of mind-altering medications and the repeated use of a cramped cell nicknamed "El Tigrito." "It's incredible to see a dictator in court," Heath said Thursday upon learning of the new charges. "The Maduro prosecution will do more to prevent the kidnapping of Americans by rogue regimes than a hundred press releases from the United Nations." Former first lady denied release for medical treatment Meanwhile, Flores' lawyers argued that Flores, 69, has medical problems that cannot be treated effectively in jail. She has lost 25 pounds (11 kilograms) while imprisoned at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn, might have suffered a minor heart attack in July, has "lingering lightheadedness, dizziness and shortness of breath" and has been told that she might need heart surgery, the attorneys said.
They also said she suffered permanent scarring when she was "thrown against a wall or dresser" during her capture. Prosecutors opposed the bail request, saying that Flores was an "extreme" flight risk and has been taken for treatment at a local hospital when needed. U.S. District Court Judge Alvin Hellerstein denied Flores' request. He noted, among other things, that she's unwilling to undergo catheterization in jail in order to determine the cause of her heart problems and the appropriate steps for treatment. He also pushed back at the notion that her high blood pressure was life threatening, noting she's already on medication for that. U.S. President Donald Trump's administration has defended the raid to capture Maduro as a "surgical law enforcement operation." Maduro has called himself a prisoner of war and his capture a kidnapping.

Published: 4:10am, 9 Oct 2026

Ousted Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores both were hit with an additional US criminal charge on Thursday stemming from accusations they tortured political opponents and American citizens to retain their grip on power in the South American country.

Separately, US District Judge Alvin Hellerstein, who is overseeing the case, denied a request by Flores to be released from jail ahead of trial due to health reasons.

Maduro and Flores were ‌charged with an additional count of conspiracy to commit torture in addition to the drug-trafficking charges they previously faced, according to a superseding indictment filed in Manhattan federal court. Maduro and Flores would face a mandatory minimum 50 years in prison if convicted.

Flores, 69, and Maduro, 63, were captured by the US military on January 3 in their Caracas home and brought to New York to face the drug charges. Venezuela has since boosted cooperation with the US under the leadership of Maduro’s former Vice-President Delcy Rodriguez.

Relations between the United States and oil-rich Venezuela were tense during the socialist Maduro’s 13 years in power. US officials and human rights groups have long accused Venezuelan officials ⁠of torturing detainees, but Thursday’s indictment marked the first time Maduro faced criminal charges over the allegations.

In one instance, prosecutors said Maduro in 2013 ordered the arrest of a Venezuelan military ‌officer he suspected of planning a coup.

Members of Venezuela’s military counter-intelligence directorate then interrogated the officer while shocking the individual with a live electric wire around 20 times and hung the individual by the hands and feet for several minutes at a time, prosecutors said.

In 2022, an American citizen ‌detained while entering Venezuela was accused of conspiring to assassinate Maduro and was tortured by military counter-intelligence officers through beatings and shocks to the person’s arms, legs ⁠and genitals, according to the indictment.

Flores stands beside lawyers Mark Donnelly and Andres Sanchez during an appearance in Manhattan federal court in New York on Thursday. Photo: Reuters

Since their ⁠capture and arrest, the US Justice Department “has been working to uncover the extent of their alleged crimes against the people of Venezuela and of the United States”, US Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a social media ‌post.

Maduro’s lawyers did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

During the court hearing on Thursday over Flores’ push to be released from jail, her lawyer Mark Donnelly said he had not had time to review the new charges with Flores. ‌Flores ‌was not asked to enter a plea.

Maduro and Flores pleaded not guilty to the drug charges and have been held at Brooklyn’s Metropolitan Detention Centre since their capture. Their trial is ‌scheduled for June 1.

Flores’ lawyers had argued their client needs a cardiac procedure and wants to recover in a more comfortable environment. The lawyers proposed moving ⁠her to a residence in the New York City area with round-the-clock private security and said she is not a danger to the community.

In denying the motion for bail, Hellerstein ⁠decided the evidence against Flores appeared strong. The judge also said Flores, who wore a dark prison T-shirt and a headset to listen to a simultaneous Spanish translation of the proceedings, appeared to be relatively healthy.

“For whatever it’s worth, her appearance today is no worse and perhaps a little better than when I first met ‌with her on her arraignment,” Hellerstein said, referring ‌to her first appearance in court on January 5.

“She was still bandaged up from the military invasion,” Donnelly said.

Prosecutors in the Manhattan US Attorney’s Office opposed Flores’ release. They said Flores has received adequate medical care at the detention centre and, if released, poses an “extreme” risk of flight and danger to the public including possible witness intimidation.

Hellerstein’s bail denial will not affect Flores’ trial or potential punishment.

Flores was Venezuela’s attorney general and led its National Assembly before becoming first lady. US prosecutors say she took hundreds of thousands of dollars in bribes from a large drug trafficker.

sources.headline: Venezuela's Nicolas Maduro and wife face new charges
sources.text: Former Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores have been charged by US authorities with conspiracy to commit torture in a new superseding indictment.

sources.headline: Nicolas Maduro, wife face torture charge in new U.S. indictment
sources.text:
By
Mark Osborne,
Updated on: October 8, 2026 / 12:07 PM EDT
/ CBS News
Add CBS News on Google
Deposed Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, are now facing an additional charge of conspiracy to commit torture as federal prosecutors filed a superseding indictment in the Southern District of New York on Thursday."As alleged in the indictment, the Maduro regime subjected over a dozen American citizens to torture while held in custody of the Venezuelan government — including drugs, electrocution, sexual assault, and more," FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement on social media. "They will now answer for their crimes."The couple were already facing a slew of charges, including narco-terrorism conspiracy; cocaine importation conspiracy; possession of machine guns and destructive devices; and conspiracy to possess machine guns and destructive devices. The 30-page superseding indictment accuses the couple of overseeing a system of political repression that relied on Venezuela's military, intelligence agencies and security forces to torture their opponents, silence dissidents and maintain power."To undermine Venezuelan democracy and entrench themselves in power, these same leaders presided over a system of repression that relied on violence against political opposition, arbitrary detention, and the torture of detainees, including United States citizens," prosecutors wrote. "That torture included electric shock, asphyxiation, rape, forced nudity, prolonged isolation, starvation, punishment cells, and psychological torture, such as threats to harm and kill victims' families, including children."
Nicolas Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, are seen in handcuffs after landing at a Manhattan helipad, escorted by heavily armed federal agents en route to a federal courthouse in Manhattan on Jan. 5, 2026.
XNY/Star Max/GC Images
Maduro and Flores were indicted by a federal grand jury in January on charges stemming from what prosecutors said was his role in a scheme to import "thousands of tons" of cocaine into the United States and enrich themselves, their family and senior members of the Venezuelan government. The U.S. military took the couple into custody in an overnight operation and brought them to the U.S. to face the charges. They have pleaded not guilty to the initial charges. Prosecutors allege Maduro ordered political opponents detained and tortured, received regular updates on interrogations and instructed officials to intensify abuse. During one briefing about a defiant prisoner, Maduro allegedly told officials to "squeeze them harder."
During political unrest in 2014, Maduro allegedly proposed abducting five to seven military officers suspected of disloyalty and extracting information through torture. According to the indictment, Flores agreed with the proposal.The indictment also includes cases involving U.S. citizens subjected to electric shocks, drowning, severe beatings and other abuse while detained in Venezuela. One American arrested in 2022 was allegedly given injections that caused seizures.A U.S. citizen detained in 2023 was severely beaten and tortured by Venezuelan intelligence officers, prosecutors said. One officer allegedly told the prisoner he had been kept alive because his U.S. citizenship made him useful in a potential prisoner exchange.
A woman walks past a mural reading "#Free Maduro and Cilia" during a demonstration in support of deposed Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, in Caracas on Jan. 16, 2026.
Pedro Mattey/AFP via Getty Images
At a bail hearing for Flores on Thursday, her lawyer asked for the arraignment on the new charge to be delayed since they just received the indictment that morning, which was allowed by the judge.
Flores' lawyer argued she should be allowed release on bail with strict conditions due to health concerns related to her heart. The judge denied bail for Flores, noting she had access to "considerable funds" and calling the charges "serious allegations."The case against the couple was brought in the Southern District of New York, where Maduro and 14 others were first indicted in March 2020, during the first Trump administration.
Sarah N. Lynch,
Jennifer Jacobs and
Jacob Rosen
contributed to this report.
In:
Nicolas Maduro
Venezuela

They have pleaded not guilty and are scheduled to go on trial starting June 1, 2027.A spokesperson for the Manhattan US Attorney’s office, which brought the charges, declined to comment.Lawyers for Maduro and Flores did not immediately respond to requests for comment.The possibility of new charges was first reported by CNN on Oct 7.Details of the new charges, including the identities of the alleged torture victims, were not immediately available.Maduro’s tenure was marked by tensions with the United States. Washington accused his government of detaining Americans as leverage to extract concessions such as relief from financial sanctions.Americans whom the US classified as wrongfully detained during Maduro’s tenure included five oil executives arrested on graft charges. They were freed in 2022 in exchange for two of Flores’ nephews, who had been convicted in the US of drug trafficking.Others detained included two former US Army Special Forces members who were arrested in Venezuela in 2020 in connection with a botched raid aimed at ousting Maduro.
